solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Aggressive goat possibly put an end to brittle toffee

blocks.note: a butter is one that butts, as a goat does
to scotch a rumour is to put an end to it

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered goat is somehow blamed for ruining a slab of toffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aggressive' looks like an adjective describing the goat; it is part of a cryptic description of a noun, BUTTER, one who butts.
explanation.definitionFit: Butterscotch is a hard, brittle toffee made with butter and brown sugar.

clue.text: Relating to plants thrown into cab

indicators.note: letters that are thrown are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Something about plants gets tossed into a taxi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' reads as a direction for where things are thrown, but it is simply four of the letters to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanic means relating to botany, the study of plants.

clue.text: Finally effect entry, dislodging new cat

indicators.note: the final letter of the next word is taken
to dislodge something is to knock it out of place, so N is removed

explanation.surface: A burglar at last forces a way in, turfing out a newly arrived cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Effect entry' reads as a single phrase about getting in, but it splits: 'Finally effect' is one letter and 'entry' is the word to be trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: A tigress is a female tiger, one of the big cats.

clue.text: Stress started by former partner’s building project?

indicators.note: the stress word is preceded, started, by the ex's letters

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner

explanation.surface: An ex-partner's building work causes nothing but stress.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as an example: an extension is one kind of building project, not a synonym for it.
explanation.definitionFit: An extension is an addition built onto a house, a typical building project.

clue.text: Divest oneself of team colours?

blocks.note: to take off, as of clothes
British for a sports team's kit in its colours

explanation.surface: A player peels off the team shirt after the match.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a sports team's kit is its strip, so 'team colours' is a noun sense sitting beside the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip is to take off one's clothes, divesting oneself of them.

clue.text: Outdoor broadcast introduced by old writer

indicators.note: O comes first, introducing the rest

blocks.note: a pen is a writer, the thing that writes
to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: An outside broadcast is presented by a veteran author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests an author, but here it is the instrument; 'old writer' does not mean a veteran novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Open-air means held outdoors, as an open-air concert.

clue.text: Wild dream of church artist involving half of High Mass

indicators.note: the church letters involve, enclose, the others
only the first half of High is used

blocks.note: m is the symbol for mass in physics

explanation.surface: A church painter fantasises during part of a High Mass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High Mass' reads as one church service, but it splits into two words doing separate jobs: half a word, and a physics symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a wild, impossible fancy, named after the monster of Greek myth.

clue.text: Deliver the goods: appear with President Adams at last?

indicators.note: only the last letter of Adams is used

blocks.note: to turn up is to appear

explanation.surface: A colon introduces the idea that success means appearing beside John Adams, the second US president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'President Adams' looks like one man; it is a president and then the last letter of Adams.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn up trumps is to come through unexpectedly well, delivering the goods.

clue.text: Out of bed, in one’s cups and on edge

blocks.note: in one's cups means drunk, and so does tight

explanation.surface: Someone is up, already drunk and jittery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In one's cups' is an old idiom for drunk; 'tight' is an informal word for the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Uptight means tense and anxious, on edge.

clue.text: Female bird initially installed in strange element

indicators.note: only the first letter of installed is used
what is installed is put inside
rum is an old word for strange

blocks.note: a hen is a female bird

explanation.surface: A hen is somehow placed inside a peculiar chemical element.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like an adjective for the element, but it is the outer word, RUM, which takes in HEN and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhenium is a rare metallic chemical element, Re.

clue.text: Perhaps part of Ben’s area separating stage belonging to TV channel

indicators.note: A comes between the other pieces, separating them

blocks.note: to mount a play is to stage it
in = belonging to, as in 'in the club'
side is dated British slang for a TV channel

explanation.surface: Ben's patch of land sits between a stage and a television station.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben is a Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis, so part of one may be a mountainside; the 's reads as 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the slope is one part of a mountain, and ben is the Scottish word for a mountain.

clue.text: Elderly relative eager for hard-wearing fabric

explanation.surface: Grandma is keen on a tough, practical cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: Nan is a British informal word for grandmother, the elderly relative here.
explanation.definitionFit: Nankeen is a durable yellowish cotton cloth, originally from Nanjing.

clue.text: Elevated plain dish — to the French

explanation.surface: A plain, raised-up dish is served French style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain dish' reads as simple food, but 'plain' belongs with 'Elevated' as the definition, a flat raised area of land.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is an area of level high ground, an elevated plain.

clue.text: Chooses photographs for the audience

indicators.note: what an audience gets is heard, not read

blocks.note: pix is informal for pictures, photographs

explanation.surface: Someone selects photos to show an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: Pix is informal shorthand for pictures, spelt the way it sounds; say it and you hear the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick is to choose, so picks means chooses.

clue.text: The writer’s left a set of books? That’s significant

blocks.note: the writer is 'I', so the writer's = I'm
port is the left side of a ship
NT = New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: An author wonders whether leaving behind a boxed set of books makes them a figure of note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer's left' looks like the writer departing; the 's is 'is' in I'M, and 'left' is the ship's side.
explanation.definitionFit: Important and significant both mean of great consequence.

clue.text: Inferior writer, one sampling The Raven, perhaps?

blocks.note: The Raven is a poem by Edgar Allan Poe, used here for its author
a taster is one who samples

explanation.surface: A second-rate writer dips into Poe's famous poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The Raven stands for its author, the way 'Shakespeare' can mean his plays; one who samples Poe is a Poe taster.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the word is a scornful term for a writer of trivial, second-rate verse.

clue.text: House in which study has unusual cerise coating

indicators.note: an unusual arrangement of the letters
the rearranged letters coat, surround, the study word

explanation.surface: A house whose study has been painted an odd cherry-red colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coating' sounds like paint on the walls, which suits cerise, but it is the instruction to surround.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a formal word for the place where someone lives.

clue.text: Central European singer regularly embracing sweetheart

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals: the 1st, 3rd and 5th
the outer letters embrace the inner word

blocks.note: S, N, E: alternate letters of singer
love = sweetheart, as a term of address

explanation.surface: A singer from central Europe holds a lover close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' looks like part of the definition, a European vocalist, but it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A Slovene is a person from Slovenia, in central Europe.

clue.text: Bad blood I attracted at first in game

indicators.note: bad letters are in the wrong order
only the first letter of attracted is used

explanation.surface: Ill feeling was drawn to me early in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad blood' is a stock phrase for enmity, which is why 'Bad' hides so well as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Diabolo is a juggling game in which a two-headed top is spun on a string between two sticks.

clue.text: Film bachelor, one embodying American book

indicators.note: to embody something is to hold it within

explanation.surface: A single man in a movie personifies a great American novel.
explanation.walkthrough: B and I, bachelor and one, hold AM and B between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Bambi is the 1942 Disney film about a young deer.

clue.text: Like our fellow countrymen’s mistake about short ceremony

indicators.note: the mistake goes around the ceremony
short means missing its last letter

blocks.note: dated UK slang for a blunder, a howler

explanation.surface: A compatriot's blunder happens during an abbreviated ritual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our fellow countrymen' is from a British setter's point of view, and the 's reads as 'has', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: For the Times setter, fellow countrymen are the British, so 'like them' is British.

clue.text: False move of young girl upset teacher’s favourite, perhaps

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset turns the word upside down, reversing it
a pet is only one example of a teacher's favourite

blocks.note: a miss is a young girl
the teacher's pet is the favourite pupil

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl's blunder spoils the teacher's pet's standing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is there because a pet is only one kind of favourite; the teacher's pet is the stock example.
explanation.definitionFit: A misstep is a false step, a mistake or wrong move.

clue.text: Going west for example, a space where boats are tied up

indicators.note: in an across clue, going west runs right to left, reversing the letters

explanation.surface: Heading west, one finds a place for boats to tie up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A space where boats are tied up' reads as one phrase, so it wants to be the whole definition; 'a space' is wordplay, and the definition is only 'where boats are tied up'.
explanation.definitionFit: A noun definition by description: the word names the place where boats are moored, rather than giving a synonym.

clue.text: Finished novel originally accepted by two press chiefs

indicators.note: only the first letter of novel is used
what is accepted is taken in

explanation.surface: A finished novel is approved by two newspaper bosses.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside the first ED: E-N-D ED. 'Chiefs' suggests first letters, but a press chief is an editor, ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Ended and finished both mean brought to a close.

clue.text: Assumed names as found in American stories

indicators.note: AS is found inside the stories word

blocks.note: stories = lies, as a child's fibs

explanation.surface: Pen names turn up in American tales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stories' means fibs, not fiction, and 'as' is simply itself, the two letters that go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: from Latin alias, 'otherwise', a name someone goes by that is not their own.

clue.text: Heavenly body wanting a treatment for asthma?

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the A is dropped

explanation.surface: A celestial object is missing a medicine for breathing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a steroid is one example of an asthma treatment, not a definition of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: corticosteroid inhalers are a standard way to calm inflamed airways.

clue.text: E.g. Oliver, extremely emaciated and bent

indicators.note: take the extremes, the first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of emaciated

explanation.surface: Oliver Twist, the starving workhouse boy, is thin and stooped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'E.g. Oliver' points to a surname shared by an example: Oliver is a Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Twisted and bent both mean out of shape.

clue.text: Again book sea transport, ringing about legal position

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it

blocks.note: to book again is to reorder

explanation.surface: A traveller rebooks a sea crossing that circles round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a volume to read, but it is the verb, to reserve. A recorder is a part-time judge in England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A recordership is the office of a recorder, a kind of judge, so a legal position.
